title: A trump is already on the table

feedback.title: A trump can be a losing card
feedback.summary: You are exactly on four. The two of Spades loses beneath North's jack of trump, letting you shed a trump without taking an unwanted fifth trick.
points: Hearts were led and your hand has none, so all three cards are legal. North has already trumped; the queen of Hearts is not winning.
You act last. The two cannot beat the jack of Spades, while your king would overtrump it and win.
The reviewed preference is to use this safe opportunity to shed a trump and retain the off-trump club. That does not prove the best remaining hand: future leads and unseen cards are unknown.

feedback.title: Overtrumping takes the trick you do not need
feedback.summary: The king beats the jack of trump and takes a fifth trick when your estimate is four. Both the two of Spades and the club would avoid this extra trick.
points: Having no Hearts allows you to trump; it does not require you to beat the trump already played.
No one acts after you, so no unseen response can rescue the king from winning this trick.
Keeping the king by losing now is not a guarantee of a final exact four; later tricks remain unresolved.

feedback.title: A safe discard, but a missed chance to shed trump
feedback.summary: The club loses to North's jack of Spades and keeps you on four for this trick. It also leaves both of your trumps in hand.
points: The club is neither the led suit nor trump, so it cannot win here.
Playing the two of Spades would also lose under the jack. The reviewed preference is to shed that trump while it is safely covered.
Discarding the club is still reasonable. Which retained hand will be easier to lose with depends on future leads and cards not shown.

author_notes: EC-043 table-evidence case: the visible JS makes undertrumping with 2S safe. Without that higher trump, the two could win. All local outcomes are determined with South last; the 2S-versus-7C preference is authored judgment, not a simulated optimal continuation.
